blocks.x: The End The End The End Mr. Alcorn, how well did you know Louis Armstrong when he was alive?

I knew Louis over 40 years. I hadn't been a professional musician to him before I met Louis. I'd go back in the old days. I'd say in the late, in the early 30s, or late 20s. I actually met Louis here in New Orleans when he came to Sublimbore. I'd say I had a chance to listen to his records way back when he first started recording the Hot Five. I didn't know Louis when he was a place here. They left and they were in different places, California, Louis and Chicago. Kenora and all of them. That's the area I came to mind.
Louis Hardin Armstrong played piano in the group. Yeah, King Oliver and all that.

But I had a chance to meet all those guys in late years. And Louis came here. The Wicked Suburban Guard. I think it was... Excuse me, where was the Suburban Guard? Right in the Sandspot, right now. Out there on the Jefferson Highway.
Right up here. By River Road?

Yeah, somewhere up in there. Louis came in here with a I think it was a ten or eleven piece of band. Chicago, because it was most of us. We had two musicians in there from locally from here. They left and gone to New York, Chicago too. We had Preston Jackson from Moncrime. Preston, he's on the... Just made a recording with me about a year ago. Just released. Oh yeah? Less than a year ago. And they had a... Bass player Johnny Lindsey, he was from here. We had Tubby Hall, he was a drummer. He was from New Orleans. And then... Louis Edward, according to him, he was from New Orleans. That's most of the guys that are here in this particular band. When they first came here, I had a chance to meet those guys. But I was playing with some old musicians that Louis had worked with. He was... Who were they? Those musicians? Oh, they were... Papa Celestine, all them guys like that. Yeah. Henry Allen's father. Henry Reed Allen's father. Alphonse Pico and all them guys. Most of all those old musicians, Louis had worked with, but I had a chance to come up with. I was pretty young when I started.
Was Pico still playing High Society then? Before he played all his days. That's a great song. Yeah.

And I had a chance to meet Louis. Well, I... How it really came about... I was working at a place called the Parish Royal. It's one of those... Swimming camps out on the lake. Mm-hmm. There was a little clarinet player Lorenzo Teo. A gentleman called Dugas, Ray Dugas. And... Walter Dugas, Piano player. And myself. And we had a couple of Bocais with us. Henry and Charlie Bocais. And we were all working out at the... At the lake. At this place, the Parish Royal. Somewhere out there where... Close to where the airport was located. And Louis... People used to go out... To the suburban garden and listen to Louis. Well, it was in the summertime. It was real hot. It didn't have air conditioning. It didn't have nothing. It just didn't have any pain. People used to go out there. And every night Louis was packing that place up. And if he was packing it in. They used to have a broadcast that would come on at 12 o'clock. At nine? Yeah. Somewhere around that time. And it broadcast Louis from the suburban garden. And quite a few of those people used to come out to the lake. And do air. When the... You know, if they come off... Got that hot place to go out to the lake to swim and cool off. They used to come... This was one of the spots they used to come to too. Mm-hm. from the San Buenville. And quite a few of those people used to come out to the lake and do air. When, you know, if they come off, got that hot place to go out to the lake to swim and cool off, they used to come, this was one of the spots they used to come to too. So quite a few people used to go out and tell them, they say, man, they got a young guy around here playing for a man, he playing some horn, you ought to hear him. And they'll say, yeah, I'd like to meet him. So we made, we set up an appointment to meet each other one night. It must have been about, it wasn't good night or it was next morning. It was about three o'clock. The building was getting off at about 12, 31 o'clock out there.
And I met him. You went from the lakefront over to the suburban?

Yeah, well, I met him in Uptown, because I always lived around Louisiana Avenue up in the city. So it was no hassle. I knew where he used to go at night. Man, you know, it was at that time. Where would they go after the suburban garden? They'd go jam someplace? No, no, they wouldn't jam. They'd go around at the time. They'd go around. And they'd go around. And they'd go around. So I met him one night. Do you remember exactly which place it was? Tickle House. Yeah. No, we first met on the, it was on Losing Avenue in Magnolia. Right there on the corner. right there on the corner. He was in his, he had a little, a little Ford, a sport mile of Ford. And he was sitting in the corner, I went over and I told him where I was. And we started talking and everything. But we had a nice conversation from that time on, you see. And he told me he'd like to hear me and everything. I told him, I said, well you can hear me, you can't come out to the lake, and you can't come out there because you're working like I am, you see. And we had-
Do you remember what year this was, exactly? Oh, um, yeah. 1930.
Yeah, that's 29 or 30. Around 30 or 29 up in there. Yeah, it'd be exactly the early part of, the last part of the 20s and the first part of the 30s, you see.
So this was the summer of 1930, you think? Yeah. Somewhere around up in there. Well, I guess the Depression had just begun by then.
Well, it was in there. Yeah. But the Depression we had before they started in the house, you know?
Yeah.

Well, I came up in the Depression. I know about the Depression. Well, was Armstrong making good money back then, during the Depression? Well, according to what things was happening at that time, you know? Good money was, I don't know what you would say called good money was-
Hundred dollars a month, I guess, something like that.
Well, he was making more money than that because he was a big name.
No, but I mean that was good money back in the Depression.
Yeah. He was making, well, he was very popular. Sure. Records were selling everywhere, every home you go in, you see it. Mm-hmm. Recorded a little.

I was talking to someone recently who told me that every time he came back, he always made it a point to go play at places where people who might not have the money to ordinarily hear him would be able to hear him.

Well, that was his idea. He would like to have done that. But one time it was a very disappointing thing. When he finished the Suburban Garden, they had a public dance that night. He ran one of them warehouses, I don't know, somewhere out there, one of them warehouses. He was going to give a big public dance that night because people had been listening to Lloyd, the broadcaster, and they announced that that night he was going to play. They had publicist and promoters who was trying to promote this thing because he figured, you know, everybody that couldn't get into the Suburban Gardens would be able to come to this public dance. And, man, I remember people was coming from, like, little towns nearby, they were kindling places like that. People coming in on horsebacks, man. Mm-hmm. There wasn't no transportation, you know, maybe a little kind of course around there and they were nearby places. People didn't have automobiles. And they were coming in like on horsebacks. It was like a big holiday. And people went out there and they were very disappointed. They canceled the dance out. Why did they cancel? It was mixed up with the promoters, some kind of promotional thing. It was all mixed up with. I don't know why it was there. I never did find the last part of that. Mm-hmm. But that was one of the most disappointing things in Lewis' life. Hmm. Because he really wanted to play. He really wanted to play for people out here, you know, that never heard him play since he had the big time and that way from here. And he wanted to play that. Now, that would have been the biggest thing that ever happened here. Why didn't he just go ahead and play?
On the contract, you see.

Oh, union. Yeah, the promoters. No, the union didn't have anything to do with that. Oh, really? No, the union wasn't involved. I was between him and the promoters and somebody here. I don't know how it was made, you see. Mm-hmm. Whenever they find, I hear the tales of that. And I think it was written, if I'm not mistaken, it was using this thing from the dock. I think the dock was there, church.
It was, you know, these walls and things in my head. Yeah.

Yeah. And, uh, we never did find out what caused that last part of that thing, but that's not going on. Hmm. And, uh, Louis was very disappointed, because he said he wanted to play for his people. He used to play his people.
Well, do you recall any times that he did give a free concert?

Well, he came back, and it was a free concert, but he came back and played at different places. At the Coliseum. He played at different places around here. He played. He came back and played. He played at most of that at the auditorium, because he'd come down and let him go, Book of Cheese. Mm-hmm.
So, uh, when you met him that night, uh, back in 1930, did you all spend a long time talking?

Yeah, we talked. We had different things we talked about, and he was very proud to see, you know, some of his eyes. Mm-hmm. Trying to keep music alive, and going to play. Mm-hmm. He was always proud of New Orleans musicians. There was nothing. You know, you know, plenty of people went up and told you they were from New Orleans. I remember it came from, uh, Baton Rouge or something. He'd say, man, I'm from New Orleans. You know, everybody was from New Orleans, indeed. Yeah. And Louie would say, man, uh, I'm a New Orleans man or something like that. Yeah. He had a good voice, but he really was dedicated to New Orleans. Louie loved everyone. He loved people, but he would never, anybody would say, I'm from New Orleans, that was it. Yeah. He was a very loyal man.
Very, very, very fireman. And, uh, that's where Louie was.

Yeah. Clean up until he left here. I mean, I had some of them last, he came down here, he played, uh, one time they had a, there's something at the, at the Royal Orleans for him. During the concert time he was down here. We went over and, uh, we played on dedicated, we went up and played at the jam, we played. Paul, Barbary and myself. Most of the guys that knew him well. Mm-hmm. We went up and played different things. When he walked in, he was, first came up to the bass, he didn't see anybody's hand before he stopped me over. No.
Do you remember what year that was? Years ago, I couldn't remember. I guess it's been a while. Yeah. Yeah. Um.
He wasn't sick or nothing at that time, though. He was, top, top shape.
Yeah. Did you ever meet his wife, Lil, Lil Harden?
You know, I never did meet Lil. Yeah. Because when I was in, uh, around Chicago, the little name of it, left way from around there, I went to Chicago in 29. I don't know where Lil had gone.
You went to Chicago in 1929. 29. Yeah. I lived, I lived with that for a short time, my mother then.

Mm-hmm. And, uh, Louis was gone. Louis was gone to New York. Uh-huh. All over all the places. I never didn't get a chance to see Louis in, in Chicago, because he had gone east. Mm-hmm. And worked around on the road, because he was always a man that went on the road all the time.
Yeah, he traveled the best.

He was saying, he traveled, always traveled. I never saw another man. No man in music ever traveled with his book. He must have loved it, though. Well, he had, uh, I guess he did love it, because everything he, anytime he put on the show, you could see he was very much pleased with what he was doing. Yeah. A guy, it could be angry, breaking the back, but when he come on that stage, full of smiles, you know, just a natural.

The reason I asked about Lil is because, uh, I've read a lot of books about him, and I kind of get the impression that she, uh, had a very strong influence. Well, she did. As a musician. She did. Lil was a fine musician herself.

And through talking with, with guys, with Lori and all them guys, the lady he is, Ed Carlton, all the musicians that we played with. She did. As a matter of fact, Lil was one of the ones that told Lil that he should go on his own.
Mm-hmm. And break with Papa Joe? And break with Papa Joe?

Oh, yeah, because he was doing plenty of things, you know. Well, Joe was the one that sent for him to come up there. Yeah. And Joe and him, uh, he was going on his own, because he, doing plenty of recording. He was like, like, some guys that were recording with the Hot Five, Johnny Dodds, and all of them. But that was an organized group. They'd get together for that, uh, just recording. That's really the only time they played was when they recorded, right?
Yeah, just recording, get together.
Mm-hmm. And recording. Or, and they were playing with different bands. But Louis was working with King Oliver, you see.
Mm-hmm. I believe he went up playing Lincoln Gardens when he left New Orleans.
Yeah, one of the most all musicians went around there was doing a pretty capital.
Yeah. I guess Buddy Bolden was before your time, right?
Oh, yeah. So Buddy Bolden died, I was pretty young when he died, because they brought him back here. My mother didn't know Buddy Bolden.
Yeah.
Oh, yeah. It's a little story, and then I was, I remember, I took on Buddy Bolden. So Buddy Bolden wrote to some, so I was getting to my mother. Oh, yeah?
Yeah, I remember.
Mm-hmm. So, uh, Buddy Bolden, see, Buddy Bolden lost his mind.
Yeah.
And they sent him.
Sent him out to a hospital. Sent him up.

They stayed up there so many years, so he was really a forgotten man. Yeah. And when this jazz started raving again, then they'd bring Buddy Bolden and then back in the picture again. Mm-hmm. But, uh, during my time coming in, the time I came up, they wasn't talking about Bolden, because everybody was talking about Louis Armstrong. Mm-hmm. Can I turn that down a little bit?

Let me just turn this off. One of the things that, uh, has interested me about the, uh, about Armstrong is that, uh, in a lot of the things he, uh, wrote himself, a lot of, uh, things about himself in his autobiography, and then also in a lot of the interviews, he talks about the sounds in New Orleans, foghorns, the bells he heard on the ships and the different ones. Yeah, just the different sounds of the city. Yeah. Do you think that, um, that those sounds still have an effect on musicians today? I don't know.
Well, you see, you didn't have automobiles. You didn't have trucks.
Mm-hmm.

You didn't have horse and wagon, and all sorts of things like that. One or two automobiles. Automobile wasn't a noisy thing. Mm-hmm. It was noisy in the calls they make it now, but, but there was nothing to interfere. It's like people used to say, how the man, the trumpet player could play. How loud he could throw their hand at five or six o'clock. Mm-hmm. You could. You didn't have these high buildings. Yeah. Like you say, Buddy Bowling. You could have Buddy Bowling planned for a mile almost. Mm-hmm. The winds traveling a certain amount of breeze coming in a certain direction, whatever's planned, and you could hear them. It didn't have no high skyscrapers. I could go on the middle of Canal Street and blow a horn out. Nobody would hear me. That's going to be right next to me.
Yeah.
Streetcars, buses, and all that. I could hear them. They made that interference. That's my idea.

How do you think sound effects musicians when a city gets bigger and bigger and you have to be closer and closer to individual sounds? I don't know if I'm saying it right, but what I'm getting at is this. When Armstrong and those cats were growing up, they could hear things a long distance away. And I think that must have influenced their sense of melody, don't you think? And rhythm and tone? Well, possible.

It's possible that it was. Yeah. Because I know that sometimes we used to be playing on the river out there, you know? Playing like maybe one of them boats. A ferry or something like that. Not only a ferry, but out there in a section. And sometimes once in a while they blow a horn and the horn had a sound. And so, there's guys play tremor with it. They just say no. Bah, bah, bah, at the same time.
Yeah.

And guys listen to all those things. You see? They had all those things going on. They had steam and the boats coming on. They always had a colliopon there. I was living way back around close to Clayton. At certain times of night we could hear a boat out there. Really? Now when was this? Was this in the 30's or 20's? Yeah, it was the 20's. I was living in the 30's. Before you started from. See you. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

Yeah. It's the Elks place now, it's called the Bowes. She could dance every Tuesday night. They had two bands playing. And there was one band on one side of the band, I know them. One band on one side of the Bowles and I know another. And one was playing on this backtown side, what he called it. Backtown, yeah. I mean, coming towards the lake. Around about 12 o'clock at night, we could hear them playing, you know. They were playing, they were playing, they were playing, they were playing.
You mean you could hear the collage? No, the instruments. Oh, the instruments. The band.
Every once in a while the breeze would blow back. And I heard that moment, I'm not telling you nothing about what I'm breathing about. I'll tell you what I know from my own.
It's a long distance.
But you see, now this is why. First thing, we didn't have that Magnolia project there.
What was there instead? Just houses?

The school, the school there, but it was a wood building. We didn't have no, these glass papers and all that stuff back up and down. And that sound could come back. It grew through bricks. So since we put up that thing, taking that wood, I'm probably just taking that area after that.
Yeah.
And that killed everything. That's why.
Do you think that sound being deadened has a bad effect on music? Do you think it causes music not to grow as well? No, I don't think so.

Because it keeps it closer to me, you know, you got to go where it's at. Mm-hmm. You know? And just like we used to could hear a woodhouse, a wood coming out. We could always tell when the parade was coming. We could hear the bass tuba. Mm-hmm. That was really, you know, penetrated over anything. And the drums. And we could hear that beat coming three or four blocks before the music would get near. Yeah. And we knew it was coming from some direction, like the drums and things. They'd come in and play the drums soft, and when they jazzed up, you could hear them play a lot. We had a bass player around. He was a lot of bass player. I was kind of Randy Jackson. He was tall, man. And you could hear his bass man over everything. Mm-hmm. But I imagine now you wouldn't hear him as full. Mm-hmm. He said, I have all this.
You know, this took me over time. Sure.
And that's what people don't understand.
Do you think there's something about music today that, in a way, compensates for the loss of sound? Or the things that work to the advantage of a musician that you didn't have many years ago?

Well, yes. Every year they improve upon things. You take thirds and record it. I know I recorded it. I have a record that I recorded at 37. It sounded good, yeah. Mm-hmm. And it was made in the thirties. But they didn't have all the mic systems back there. A couple of mics didn't do it. Now they got everything. Back in the room in the hotel and records. You see? That's nice. Equipment wasn't picking up like it. It was made a good song. It was the Sammy Lewis records. They're back in the English. Yeah.
A lot of the Hot Five records are good today. Good today.
From that sound. But if they recorded it, they're looking for Sammy there. But they didn't prove it on the sound. Yeah. Put everybody on a different track. Sure.
I guess it really gives you a better sense of all the harmony. Sure.

But not today. I mean, back in the old days people just had the night or summer record play. They would go in the old dance hall and record. Not record you command, the guy command. You can do anything to take. 40 years they put it out. I got a record like that. We made it in the Pedder. It sounded very bad. Down in the French court?
Yeah. Yeah.

Yeah. But a guy came in a Pedder. I can remember. Sometime he got a tape in the 80s and released him. The office picked him or something like that. But you could see where he had something. But it would have been better if it had been recorded. You know, that's the guy had mics and everything. They took him one of them and went to the world for a long distance. Wow.
When you mentioned funerals, that's something I'm curious about. Do you recall Armstrong playing any funerals back then?
No, he wasn't playing no parades or nothing like that. He never played a parade again? No, he did that. Everybody knew him playing a parade again. No, I mean when he came back.
After he had made it big. No, no.

Because the last thing I was doing was when he was King of the Zool. I was playing with old man Allen. The great Allen's father. But when he was the king. He was on the floor just enjoying the music. He was right behind him with the music. Yeah. When he came out and played concerts. Uh huh. He played all the children in different places.
Do you remember some of the better concerts? With Lloyd?

Yeah. I thought every concert Lloyd put on with a little bit. Yeah. Even when we were on the floor. We used to run with each other. And I left here at 32. I joined Don Howard's band. I was in San Antonio. Lloyd came through. It was a big band. And we was off that night. We ran in. And of course the whole band was. Who wanted to do. Yeah. All musicians were coming in. And we came down with a ton. And we were living there at some time. He was there to see us. Every show. I never saw Lloyd put on a bed. Yeah. The man was a natural. Everything he did was a natural. Yeah. One time I was in Vegas. I was working in Vegas with some guys. Lil was working around in Vegas. We used to meet every night. At the Moreland Rules. Probably at that time. We were going over to. Matter of fact we were all living in the hotel. We were living out there. We used to meet each other. We'd get off at Mason time. We'd get off around 4 o'clock. I'd say we'd meet about 2 o'clock. Yeah. We had to live for Oakland to Oakland to Oakland. We both used to like gin, gin tonic Gin tonic? Yeah, we used to sit around drinking a few now Yeah He was not receiving this He really loved to live, didn't he? Yeah, it might be Because he used to say alcohol and say we were going to have breakfast I said, well I'll leave He said, well, Lamar, Lamar, you make rain and tell all the guys But all the guys we had, help man, was from New Orleans Yeah But the guys in his pay, I wouldn't for him So he felt close, he loved his man, but he was born to be like Phil Matthews Happy Ghosts All them guys knew when he was a boy, they all played around here together And it was a good thing for him to be together That's an honor
I guess New Orleans was really always a part of his temper and his style every place he went

Oh yeah, well, but See, when Kid Ory had this thing going on before either King Oliver was playing with Ory And when Oliver got a chance to go to New York, Chicago Ory was a young fellow player around here He used to hang around with him all the time Go around, he used to fame So he said, get that boy He was a young man, he said, get a kid They called him a kid too Everybody, when he was young, they called him a kid He would take that name, some guys kept that name going Kid so and so Ory never wanted to be a kid To them, they called him youngster kids And They got Louie in the band Good baby, let him talk I thought he would come around here And I went to Boat Played on his kid, I said, with Freed and all And he left my own tour He always sent for him Did you know Baby Dodge?
Oh yeah
Baby and Terry Daz too
Yeah I've been reading this book Shining Trumpets about jazz This guy says he thinks Baby Dodge Is the greatest jazz drummer ever lived You think that's true? Well I tell you

He was a great drummer Those guys had a certain thing with these New Orleans drummers Down there originally Most of the New Orleans drummers had something Like Paul Barker All the drummers here had a certain beat Kept this thing going on Down in New Orleans It was a certain thing Yeah All the guys had that certain thing And that's where the guys just allowed to do all the drummers So That's the way it was Paul Barker
Do you think Baby Dodge was better than those people? Or do you Well I would say

Because they were both All of them was good at what they were doing Just like drummers players Just they were the best drummers player Just they were the best sex drummers player So the guys had their style of play
You don't put Lewis a notch above the others then?

I say Lewis was the greatest because he was a starlet He had his own way of playing And he was the guy that turned his trim He made the sound of the trumpet They had good trumpet players back in the years
But he was the one who really opened it up Got that trance on him
The thing that he had he had something like the whole world from him Yeah
Just like a singer

A singer would get a star Then Lewis came along singing and playing and everything else And he just changed the whole pattern and everything He had Bing Crosby in the middle of the singing that he did Yeah
Yeah
He was more famous than Bing Crosby in the middle of the night Because he was born in the middle of the night Oh I think he still is
Oh yeah

But I mean I'm just saying He was a natural Bing Crosby was singing with the boys And the Lutheran still with Paul White But I mean He was a soloist and artist out there How did he get the nickname Pops?
Just a nickname
Some of them used to call him Satchim O Satchim O
Yeah

I knew that The guys pick up all kinds of names If you listen to them Yeah And you answer to them That's going to be your name I had many names called But I don't take them Just an hour and hour point I don't get too much for this Yeah
Let me This is about to finish Let me just turn it over
When did you next see him after that time in 1930 in New Orleans? When was the next time that...
Yeah, after that time you saw him that night.

Well, I left waiting here without I was band. We had a travel band. We used to run into each other over. San Antonio, we would meet in different places. We met in Miami. Wherever they'd be playing, different places we'd always run into.
This was all during the 30s? Yeah, all bands was running over each other in the 30s. Yeah.
We had everybody out on the board. We was running over each other. All bands out there.
Were you living out of Chicago then or New Orleans?

No. Well, this was always my home man. I never really kept up my home then. But I lived in San Antonio at that time. We were working in San Antonio. That was our headquarters. We were down in the out of Spain. And the agencies used to book us, you see. We were going over to West Virginia. We were some time we played. Two nights. A night in the town. Two bands. You see, running. Cab Calloway, Duke. Tom Redden, the only big band.
Do you think you all were well paid back in those days?
I don't know if they were well paid.
No. You could say the fact that it was the Depression and a lot of folks were just not eating.
That's right. But I don't say we were well paid but it wasn't happening.
What would you make on an average night?

Well, you see, we was talking about on the bus. Mm-hmm. First time we try to do some time. We do pretty nice on the night. We run and the bus will really end out. And what? The rear end of the bus jump out. Get all that fixed up. You had nothing but headaches, you know? Oh, man. It was something. Bus out, one of them big old greenhouse bus tires. That's $150. Back in the Depression almost. Man. So, I mean, you see, it was just nothing wasn't. Many guys got disgusted in that out of here.
Yeah.
Some guys went into the professor and doctors and all these things. They just got on for the day.
Yeah.

Some of those stubborn guys we stayed with. I mean, that was 50 years ago. It's a long time. Did you ever... Put it down. Did you ever play with Louie in this group? No, I had a chance to go with Louie. When Louie came from here, Louie tried to get me to come in the band then. I used to be a first trumpet player too.
When was this now? Um... Still in the thirties? Forties? Forties? Yeah.

It had Louie Russell's band back then. Um... Um... Because Louie used to be a band all the time. He would... Well, he would sing all things. He would sing all things. He would sing all things by himself. He would tell you what he would be. And Louie Russell's band kept going on. So they came from here and Louie told me, Sabbath one, he said, Oh, the phone had a... I said, man, Sabbath one. They had two bands tonight. Their band was playing out again. They were sitting in the desk. And he said, They were talking to me. They were talking to me. They were talking to me. They were talking to me. They were talking to me. So... I looked into the band. And he said, We got a Troublem player. We got a Troublem player. For Troublem player. For their skates. For their Troublem player. So he had a Louie Russell Wilson line. That was two Troublem players. I said yeah, the Louis Russell wants to mind the upskins, he said, two trips. I said, why don't you come here and do it? I said, well, I've been out there, man. I've got seven, eight years. I've been going on that road. They've got to keep doing them going all the time in one night. They go on a regular job and stay a week, that's a long time. It cost so much money to hold a band like that. So, trying to do spots could have folded half, Louis was going to be a big band in there. So, I told him, I said, well, that was one of the first times, one of the greatest things I've ever had. Louis asked me to come down from the band.
That is quite a compliment. It was, you see.

And I thought it was great, but I said, well, this one time Louis asked me, I had to discipline. Because I never, I always thought from when I first started, I was praying. And someday I'd play with all those guys. I used to say it all the time. So, someday I'll play with those guys. And during the 15th tournament, I played with everyone. You see. And I was saying that as a youngster, maybe I was talking from the top of my head, but I was, I know they were so great over me and so far up over me, I didn't, I thought someday I'd be good enough to play with them. You see. But that's your dream. So, I didn't wake up, I just kept on dreaming or anything. But he did ask me to do that.
What do you think was the best period of his musical career? When was the, when were the best years when he played music? What do you think?

Well, Louis had so many good, good, mixed in spots. Because I was crazy about, first thing everybody was crazy about the Hot Five. Never had another thing like that. Everybody tried to organize things, but they never got them close to the Hot Five. The Oriole and Johnny Giles. Yeah.
Little St. Cyr I think was in the place.

Johnny St. Cyr, yeah. And they never, guys copy their records a day. Something that, even if they played a solo just like him, it's not those guys. Sam Ray Orr, Orr has got things on the drum hall. Jack Keegan on the room used to come sit down and listen to him. He said, old man, that's it. He used to speak about, Trumma Young used to come follow us around all the time. He said, Orr, you got something. What does this old man have? He said, the guys just had something happen. It was just what you call leaders. You know, guys, what they're doing, it was guys that everybody could set a pattern out.
I think Billie Holiday was that way as a singer.

Yeah, quite a few people set patterns after Billie Holiday. Billie Holiday came in the late years. Billie Holiday came in the school president. I'm sorry. During the time of, my time or something. She wasn't old as me when she died. I'm just saying, you know.
She was that same kind of natural though as an artist, don't you?
I came through with that. But the one that said everything was Bessie Smith and other people. See, back in those days we had blues singers like Bessie Smith. Ma Rainey.
Ma Rainey.
Paul Rainey and all the women like that. Yeah. They really were setting pace for blues. And that's how these young singers like Billie Holiday had one pattern out there.

Do you think that Armstrong's music grew less and less as he got older? Or did you see him make dramatic changes in his later years in his stuff? You know, Hello Dolly is a much different song from something like starting with some barbecue.
Well, Louis did. Louis used to like to play pop latoons as well as, yeah. Many people wanted Louis to go back and play things that he played 50 years.
Louis said that.

Yeah. Sometimes he wouldn't do any of them things. Mahogany Hall Stone, fireworks, all them things like that. Louis played that when he was a young man. A man, he could still play them, you see. But he was trying to keep, he was a leader. He was trying to get some man keep things going away at a time, you know. He didn't try to sound 40 years old, he wouldn't have been a little strong if he'd been playing the same thing. Who was going to hear him? Yeah. I mean people like to hear you come in and play that thing. But just like you go back to that area back there, that's all right for somebody that just don't sound like him, but he want to go on so he can keep on going. There wasn't no limit to this man.
Yeah. Do you think that his music changed when he had a big band backup as opposed to the small groups he played with when he was young?

Well it was a different, sure quite natural, because the melodies of tunes had changed. God was writing songs with like body and soul and all that beautiful songs like that. And he was playing, he liked to play beautiful ones, make beautiful changes. And the big bands put in, well you see when he went to Hot Five he was playing with five men, everybody for themselves. Yeah. But then he got five, six saxophones on them, he was playing melody to that, fighting and all that, and different things like that. He had to change. A guy like that he couldn't move back.
Yeah. He didn't like bop music very much, did he? What do you mean bop? Well, you know the music that came along during the fifties that was...

Oh. He never tried to play that. Uh huh. Because he had his way of playing. And Louis, all them guys was playing bop, used to sit down and try to play Louis, dizzing all of them. Yeah. They lived all for Louis, Roy Aldrich all of them. I got records, I got everything they did, I don't care what they play on them, Louis Armstrong is in it. Yeah.
I guess he's really the father of all of you, isn't he? Father of the world.
Man said, please, you listen to Bunny Berrigan. Can't get started. Uh huh. What is it?
Louis and A? Uh huh. You really see him in all the music that's come, come since him.
And he's still falling back on Louis, yeah.
Yeah. And was it that he, I think in the last few years of his life, he refused to come back to New Orleans, didn't he? Uh huh.

Didn't he? Well, after this big thing came up, that big disappointment in the head, he wasn't too particular about coming back for a while. You see, he really felt bad. And he couldn't play for his people and call his people to New Orleans.
Yeah. But that was back in the thirties, wasn't it?
Yeah, he still lived that in his heart too.
Yeah.

See, because there was a big disappointment to Louis. Louis was good. Louis, the money wasn't involved, Louis would pay that night for nothing. Sure. People know Louis. People would pay that night for nothing to get out there and play for them people. Louis was raised up with guys like had these first Zulu clubs. That first club we started. Those fellows was his friends. They used to follow him around. And he couldn't perform for them like he wanted that night. And that was the biggest disappointment in New Orleans for Louis in his life. And it took a while for Louis to live that down. You know what I'm saying? But I would have been living, I would have been the same way.
Anybody else. But he continued to come back throughout his life, didn't he? He came back. How often would he come back?
Well, he'd get booked back. Yeah, he came down here with the Zulus. He was the king with the Zulus.
That was 49, I believe. Yeah, king with the Zulus.
And he came back and played different things. He came back off to the New Orleans back every day. We're looking this way, you know?
Would he come back once a year or less than that? Maybe not that much. Maybe not that much. Yeah.
But that was the biggest disappointment to Louis. Uh-huh. And Louis cried that night. It was quick. It really helped.
Where did you all go after? After that thing?

Yeah. Everybody walked with the heels down. Came home with the sand. Looked like a fume. Looked like a blue head died or something, man. Because it couldn't end. Yeah. That's how the people was coming back, man. People came from all out in the country.
Who were the... You said it was the promoters? Did the law have anything to do with it?

I don't know what it was. We never found out that. I know they didn't have it that night. Uh-huh. I waited for some guys to tell you. But you had so many tears on it. Yeah. I'm just telling you it was a disappointment. Sure.
I can imagine.

I wouldn't add on to it what it was. But they said it was... I know he was hurt because he wanted to play. And they was announcing that people was buying tickets and getting things together. Women was buying dresses to go to that that night. And that took the pressure, man.
People were poor.
Yeah.
Yeah.
And it was really...
People wanted to have a look. Yeah.
He was disappointed in himself. But money didn't mean nothing to him on that.
Yeah. Yeah.
The boys would have gotten richer on it though.
Uh... But as I understand that he didn't... He didn't come back to New Orleans or did... Didn't he publicly state that he wouldn't come back to New Orleans in his last years or something like that?
No, I didn't... I couldn't say that. No.
Because he was very angry at New Orleans when he died. Not, of course, his people but the city, I think, for the segregationist policies and things like that.

Well, plenty of things. You see, Louis, when Louis came out here, Louis came back with a mixed band. He thought that wasn't... That's what he said. All kind of laws on that. He could play everywhere, but with New Orleans, they didn't want no mixed band. And all that kind of thing. It was very disappointing because he had that kind of chore.
And this was in the 50s or 60s? It was recently.

It almost looked like yesterday, you know? Really? You know how this thing changed. Yeah. I guess it was what? Mid 60s, something like that. Yeah. But Louis, Jack Keek, all of them... Jack Keek, all of them came out here and played with Louis. He was playing the same band. Mm-hmm. Came here with him. But the place he was going, he was going to Texas, he didn't have no trouble. Down here, there was a little... A little... A question of feeling about it, you know? Yeah.
Do you think the city has changed much in its attitude toward jazz musicians? Certainly, y'all get more work, I think, than... Oh, yeah.

It's changed. It's changed plenty in everything. The way of life has changed. Everything changed. Everybody got to wake up. The people here got to wake up. Yeah. And New Orleans is a better town in many places. I think so. See? I'm born in red here. I saw the trend change. I know all about New Orleans. My mother and all of them was born here. We didn't come here from... From Buccaloza or... I see they protested. Even out here. We born my mother and all of them raised in the garden district right there. Wasn't that sexy where you had out there?
Yeah.
Thirst Street. See?
And we know New Orleans. I know New Orleans.

All my days I was in New Orleans. When Calton was a town that saw me. This was a sexy town. My mother and them was in New Orleans. Not in Calton, they was in New Orleans. I didn't move up in Calton until... I had my family. Hmm. Twenty-some-odd years ago. Twenty-eight years ago. But that's the way it was. We knew. Every body by business. Yeah, I think it's one of the good things about the city. It's got that kind of tightness. There's a lot of flow in and out of different families and lives and things like that. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. a lot of flow in and out of different families and lives and things like that. That's right. That's important I think, not only for musicians but everybody.
For people. You'd be surprised how people related to him.
That's something that really comes through in Armstrong's music I think, you know, that warmth and that feeling for the people. Really he was a very passionate man. That's right.
But he was... I could sit on and talk about a little more, man, you know? Because we had so many things in common ourselves, Lou and I.
Yeah.

We were very good friends. I don't know, don't forget in 1954 I went to California. I was working with Kid Ora to hang over. Lou used to come there and play that town, play concert that town. When he'd get off that night he'd come right there. He'd sit down at the ball, stand behind the ball. Sit over there on the side where I'd be playing, you know? Waiting for him to get out and go talk. How you doing? Yeah. Telling me how I would talk.
Yeah.

But he was good friends. He'd start getting a little mixed up with dreams for a long time. Mm-hmm. So he'd waste all this time telling me, You're still crazy about it? He'd say, How come? I'd say, You know what I'm doing? I don't know how you're in the business way. I'm supposed to be out of there. I'd say, Why you sit up there? I'd say, You got some money out there for your band. I got a better band. He'd say, I've got a better band right here. He'd say, Boy, it's a band together. Mm-hmm. I got all individuals. He'd say, But I'd like to make up his mind. And it's a book of them. It's what I'd bring home to Europe. It's a success in Europe. He'd say, They even want over in Europe. He didn't want to go. He didn't go to Europe all these many years. So I went with him in 56. That's when we went to Europe. Boy, he should never been to Europe. I went with him in 56. Why was that? Why did he? Look how young I was under there. Yeah. He should have been to Europe 10 times before I was born. That's how this didn't go nowhere. Hmm. Went to California and he stayed there. Left to California and went to California and I would leave.
Mm-hmm. He never returned to New Orleans. Not to live.

Or it came through here in 1956. He was going to Europe. And Or it came by train from here to New York. He wouldn't ride the plane. He didn't get much for planes. He had to ride the plane later. So he came through here with his family. And he didn't get off the train. That's what I understand. This train went on New York. When I got to New York, I flew from here to New York. To go meet the ship. We went up on the SS plan. We was coming from different areas. Because we had taken a break. The band was off for a while. You see. We got this trip to go. And some of the guys came from California. They went direct from California to San Francisco and over. I came from New Orleans, New York and over. And that's the way I went. And Norrie came through here on the plane. I mean on a train. I went to New York with his family. And we all was on the same ship called SS Flammers.
And when was this? 1956. 1956. First trip he made over there.

Louis had been over there for years. You know, going back and forth. Bechet was over there. All of them were glad to see us when we got over. Sidney Bechet? Oh yeah, he was living there. Where did he live?
Paris?

Paris. When I was close, he had a pillar out there. He was very popular. And we met promoters over there. Guys playing countries. The guy said one thing about Louis. He said, all we do is count the people standing up. We don't have to worry about this. Every seed is sold. Every time he plays. The guy in Paris told you this? Yeah. All over Europe. Everywhere Louis played. With Louis. He said, let's just pay four thousand people. It's four thousand people. See it. All he had to do is see how many are standing up. Count to one. Everything was a side seat. He was a natural man.
Clean up until he died.

Never had a band concert. He was a favorite. The Europeans were crazy about that. Yeah. I know he lived in Paris. Yeah. He lived in Paris. Yeah. He lived in Paris. He lived in Paris. He lived in Paris. He lived in Paris. He lived in Paris.
He lived in Paris. ! 1934 I believe during the summer time.

Yeah, well he went over there and played and worked headquarter out of there. You see, the town of Haiti just like we headquartered out of there. We knew the Corporation of America, M.C.A. And that was our headquarters. We broke all around. I went around about ten, twelve countries. How long were you over there, 50 cents? We were supposed to stay five months or four months ago. I think we stayed about three months or four.
When did you go over there? What time of year?
Went over there almost this year.
So it was...
Right around, close to Christmas.
Close to Christmas. Yeah, close to Christmas. November or something like that. And when did you come back? After New Years?

I think all of my holidays at that time, I think I was over there. I can remember getting a new feeling seeing the little Christmas decorations. Yeah. So used to celebrating it at home. Sure. But that was it. We were always over there. We wouldn't be in the same town or same state, the same country. We would be in Germany, we would be in England. Something like that. We would always know how to keep them things going.
Oh yeah. Because they don't run no bands into each other. Yeah. Did he listen to much classical music? Do you know?
I didn't know classical music. No, I said Louis.
Louis? Yeah. Oh, I imagine that he liked it.

Because Louis liked this and any kind of music. And he carried a few records around with him and everything like that. He said I listened to all that. What kind of... Do you know what kind of... Not that he played too much classical music, but he used to listen to all that. I listen to classical music. I don't play classical music.
What kind of classical music do you like particularly?

Well to be honest with you, I said I listen to symphony music. Beethoven? Yeah. Anything like that because there's movements in there. Mm-hmm. We can get something out of it. Sure. You see? And I love to hear that.
Mm-hmm.

Yeah. Just like something we play when you put little raps down like that. Blah, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah. Some of the things I play like that I have a little... Full, full measures of it. You know? And add it into jazz. Put it into a song. That's what it is. The way you feel. Now Louis can sit down and play Tiger Rag and mix it about ten different songs.
Hm.
You know? When doing the solo. Yeah. Da, all that kind of different little things. The melodies you hear from other songs. Look what is it? They come out with the songs.
Uh-huh.
And that's where the jazz thing comes in. That's a, you know, individual thing. Yeah.
Yeah. Were Sidney Bechet and Louis Armstrong pretty good friends? Oh yeah.
Well they're all boys around here, you see? Yeah. They come up and all...
You mean did they remain friends all through life?

Yeah. They did, you know? Uh-huh. Sometimes you guys have a little thing they don't like. Sometimes they... I'm sorry. They died friends. I mean you made like a little arguments or something. Oh well no. But I mean they're all friends.
Why did Bechet stay in Paris? Didn't want to come back at all?

Well Sidney was around New York. He was doing alright in New York. But he went over in that foreign country over there. That's what made him so big. He went over there. He had been going over there for years. Uh-huh. And he decided to stay over there. Well he was like a king over there. And that would have been a big man in this country like he's over there.
Uh-huh.
That's what he was. It was a big thing.
Did you know any of uh... Either of Louis' two last wives, Velma or uh... Uh uh... This one he had now? Uh... Lucille.

Lucille? Yeah. Yeah he had another one on here too. Used to travel with him during the 30's. They had Alva. A little short one. A little grounski one. Alva. And uh... Of course there was Lil. Yeah well Lil. Lil. He had been away from Lil. But he had Alva since then. And then Lucille came up. Uh-huh. I knew them. I really had more to be around in that. Yeah. Yeah. And then Lucille came up. Uh-huh. I knew them. I really had more to be around in that. Yeah. Now were they musicians too? Alva I think she was still a little singer. But I don't know if she sang with a dancer or singer. Something like that. Some kind of musical thing. Unless she worked on some jobs. But Lucille used to be a professional dancer. She was dancing at cotton club. Oh. She was Lil Louis playing her. She lived around New York. She's very well known.
She's still alive. Oh yeah. Do you know her very well? Very well. Yeah. I see her every time she comes around here.
Does she come down here very well? Yeah. She came around here. Or... Yeah. To go for the zoos. Oh, right. She'll come around here.
Do you have her address where I might be able to ride her?

No. I tell you who to get that address from. Uh-huh. From the Jazz Museum. Jazz Museum. Yeah. Somebody has it because they keep in touch with them all the time. In the New Orleans Jazz Club they keep in touch with her. Dick Allen knows in New Orleans. Yeah, I'll ask him.
Yeah. They know how to keep in touch with her.
See her because they see her when she come in here all the time. Uh-huh.

Do you think... Yeah. I was going to ask you if you thought Louis was... You know, we were talking a little bit earlier about sounds, how sounds in New Orleans affected those musicians back in the old days. Do you think that having spent so many years in Chicago... We got a little bit left. We got a little bit left. Having spent so many years in Chicago and New York that the sounds of those cities might have affected him. You know, like the traffic and the rail and the subway, things like that. No.
No. I don't think that would affect him. Just like it doesn't affect us, I could be blowing in the air. But an airplane that plays over my head, that doesn't take nothing from me.

What I mean is, at times when you're not playing, when you're walking the streets and you hear those sounds, do you think they have a positive effect or is it just something you just try to not have bother you? I'm just wondering how sounds, all kinds of sounds affect a musician. I don't know.

Because they never take an effect on me as individual, you know. Sure. If it's a noise, it's a noise. If it's this or that, or something like that, it doesn't distract me. I just got so now I could be playing, keep talking, it doesn't worry me anymore. It used to bother me. You know, you got to do, you got to do something. You got to do something. Plenty of places you go, you know, things open, you can't walk in there during that time. When you guys don't show up, they got to do that, don't you? You don't walk in this front door when he's on the stage, don't you? You know, you sneak in through the back, but you're not going to do that front door. You know, how many people out there, they don't let him in with his show?
You got it like that, don't you? When was the last time you saw Louie? Louie.

Last time Louie came from here? Yeah, I can't do it. Do it jazz time? Something around the other half of Louie. He came in town for that. Was that the one I don't know what he was going to get? Is that the one I don't know what he was going to get? Is that the one I don't know what he was going to get? Is that the one I'm going to get? Sometimes I couldn't be that because you know it's pretty good. I don't know. Somebody knows things past, not thinking. You see, you don't think about those things after a guy passed when the last time you saw him, when the last time you talked with him. I never thought, never pictured Louie being dead even now. Did you go up to New York for a shoot? No. I just saw him with my son for the hip. I wasn't too particular about seeing him being here. I like to keep the brain of his life. I think he still is. Yeah, that's what I do. When I have a little things around here, in a few minutes I'm going back and get a picture and things with him. He was in Canada and so on. I still write my cards all the time. Do you have some of those cards? They say I have a photo of them right now. I don't have a bit. I'll go get it.
Okay.
New Orleans and Louisiana, everybody, if you'd like to tell you anything about many other bands.

Maybe we can do another reel, huh? And talk about Mississippi musicians. Of course, I want to talk about a lot of people. Like where Bert Sigerson is now. To find him, you reminded me of that. What Sidney Ayrton used to call a BAME system clarinet, what he called an ALBA system. Yeah. What did you say it was?

Well, Sidney referred to the ALBA system clarinet as a few key. He referred to the BAME system clarinet, which had so many more keys, as a thousand-legged clarinet. And, of course, Sidney was extremely interesting to me. And he played in South Louisiana with a little dance down there for years. He played with Joe Rivette. And Joe Rivette was very famous to that part of Louisiana in the 30s. Sidney, well, they used to have a little slogan, it's a swingin' sweat with Joe Rivette. He later became a gambler, a professional gambler, was in Las Vegas for a long period of years. But he was a good guitarist. Well, who was the leader of that band? It was Freddie Newman's band. Freddie Newman's band. Freddie Newman's band. Freddie had stayed on, Sharky and Monk Hazel. Yeah. And Nina had quit, but Monk Hazel, there wasn't anything else to do. So they wanted to work, and so they had stayed on at this little Silver Slipper. It was just below 327. It must have been in the 400 block of Burbank. It may have been in the 300 block, I can't be sure.

I swear I heard... Excuse me, go ahead. That's where I interviewed Jack and where I interviewed Noxy. No kidding. Yeah. You know, and eventually the name of it changed. And it eventually became one of these banjo places your father's playing.

segments.title: How well Alcorn knew Armstrong; Louis's band at Suburban Gardens
segments.summary: Alcorn says he knew Louis over 40 years, and describes the Chicago band that came to the Suburban Gardens, its New Orleans members, and the old musicians he played with.

segments.title: Meeting Armstrong on Louisiana Avenue, summer 1930
segments.summary: Working at Parish Royal on the lake, Alcorn hears of Louis packing the Suburban Garden and they meet one night on Louisiana Avenue in 1929-30.

segments.title: Armstrong's money and popularity during the Depression
segments.summary: Discussion of whether Armstrong made good money in the Depression; he was a big name and records sold everywhere.

segments.title: The cancelled public dance that disappointed Armstrong
segments.summary: Alcorn tells how a big public dance planned for Louis at a warehouse was canceled amid promoter trouble, and how crowds came on horseback for nothing.

segments.title: Armstrong's loyalty to New Orleans and a later jam at the Royal Orleans
segments.summary: Their first talk, Louis's pride in New Orleans musicians, and a later jam with Paul Barbarin when Louis visited.

segments.chapter: Lil, Oliver and the Hot Five
segments.title: Never meeting Lil; Chicago in 1929 and Armstrong on the road
segments.summary: Alcorn never met Lil Armstrong; he was in Chicago in 1929 while Louis was already east, and comments on Louis always traveling.

segments.chapter: Lil, Oliver and the Hot Five
segments.title: Lil's influence and Armstrong leaving King Oliver for the Hot Five
segments.summary: Lil was a fine musician who urged Louis to go on his own; discussion of the Hot Five as a recording group and Louis with Oliver.

segments.chapter: Lil, Oliver and the Hot Five
segments.title: Buddy Bolden's fate and Armstrong's fame in Alcorn's youth
segments.summary: Alcorn recalls Bolden losing his mind and being forgotten, while everybody in his time talked about Louis Armstrong.

segments.chapter: Sounds and recording in old New Orleans
segments.title: Sounds of old New Orleans and their effect on musicians
segments.summary: Asked about Armstrong's accounts of city sounds, Alcorn says there was little noise, horns carried far, and river boats and calliopes were heard.

segments.chapter: Sounds and recording in old New Orleans
segments.title: Hearing bands and parades from afar before the Magnolia project
segments.summary: Alcorn recalls hearing dance bands, parade drums and bass tuba from blocks away, which the new buildings killed.

segments.chapter: Sounds and recording in old New Orleans
segments.title: Recording technology then and now
segments.summary: Alcorn compares thin early microphones with modern multi-track recording, and mentions old records made in dance halls.

segments.chapter: Sounds and recording in old New Orleans
segments.title: Whether Armstrong played parades and funerals after fame
segments.summary: Armstrong did not play parades when he came back; Alcorn recalls him as King of the Zulus and giving concerts.

segments.title: Running into Armstrong on the road and drinking gin in the 1930s
segments.summary: After joining Don Albert's band in 1932, Alcorn met Louis in San Antonio and elsewhere; they socialised, and Louis loved his New Orleans friends.

segments.title: Ory, Oliver and Louis's start; Baby Dodds and New Orleans drummers
segments.summary: How Ory and Oliver brought Louis into the band, followed by opinion on Baby Dodds and the New Orleans drummers' beat.

segments.title: Why Armstrong was the greatest; Bing Crosby and nicknames
segments.summary: Alcorn calls Louis the greatest because he changed the pattern of singing and playing, and discusses the nickname Pops or Satchmo.

segments.title: Meeting up with Armstrong on the road in the 1930s
segments.summary: Alcorn says bands constantly ran into each other on tour across the country in the 1930s.

segments.title: Touring from San Antonio, pay and bus troubles in the Depression
segments.summary: Alcorn's band was based in San Antonio, booked by agencies; pay was poor and bus repairs were costly.

segments.title: Armstrong asking Alcorn to join his band
segments.summary: Louis tried to recruit Alcorn for his band in the 1940s, and Alcorn declined; he had dreamed of playing with such men.

segments.title: The best Armstrong period: the Hot Five; Billie Holiday and the blues singers
segments.summary: Alcorn praises the Hot Five as unmatched, and the talk turns to pattern-setting singers such as Billie Holiday, Bessie Smith and Ma Rainey.

segments.title: How Armstrong's music changed with big bands; his view of bop
segments.summary: Louis played pop tunes and had to change when playing with big bands; he did not play bop, but bop players studied him.

segments.chapter: The cancelled dance and race in New Orleans
segments.title: Armstrong's lasting hurt over the cancelled dance
segments.summary: Alcorn explains Louis was reluctant to return for a while after the big disappointment, and later came back as King of the Zulus.

segments.chapter: The cancelled dance and race in New Orleans
segments.title: What happened that night and the crowd's reaction
segments.summary: Alcorn describes the crowd going home crushed, the unknown cause and the poor people who had bought tickets.

segments.chapter: The cancelled dance and race in New Orleans
segments.title: Armstrong's anger over segregation and the mixed band
segments.summary: Louis came back with a mixed band and met resistance from New Orleans laws and attitudes in the mid-1960s.

segments.chapter: The cancelled dance and race in New Orleans
segments.title: How New Orleans has changed; Alcorn's family roots
segments.summary: Alcorn says the city has changed for the better, describes his family born in New Orleans and the closeness of its people.

segments.title: Friendship with Armstrong in California in 1954
segments.summary: Alcorn describes Louis visiting him when he worked with Kid Ory in California, and their banter about bands.

segments.title: The 1956 trip to Europe with Armstrong
segments.summary: Alcorn recounts sailing to Europe in 1956, Paris and Bechet, promoters counting standing crowds, and touring ten or twelve countries over the holidays.

segments.title: Armstrong and classical music; blending melodies in jazz solos
segments.summary: Alcorn says Louis listened to all music and he himself likes symphonies; Louis could mix tunes into Tiger Rag.

segments.title: Sidney Bechet's friendship with Armstrong and staying in Paris
segments.summary: Bechet and Armstrong stayed friends, and Bechet remained in Europe where he was like a king.

segments.title: Armstrong's wives Alva and Lucille
segments.summary: Alcorn names Louis's later wives, Alva and Lucille, says Lucille was a dancer, and suggests who has her address.

segments.title: Whether city sounds affected musicians
segments.summary: Alcorn says noises do not affect him as a player and he can play through distractions.

segments.title: Last time Alcorn saw Armstrong
segments.summary: Alcorn cannot recall the last time he saw Louis, cannot picture him dead, and offers to fetch photographs and cards.

segments.title: Fragment of a different recording on Louisiana musicians
segments.summary: An unidentified voice and questioner discuss clarinet systems, Joe Rivette, Freddie Neumann's band at the Silver Slipper and an earlier interview.
